subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

section_titles: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
periods.activity_title: Animal Hops: Counting in Equal Steps on a Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Frog jumps 3 steps at a time. Which numbers will the frog touch? Will it touch 67?
Squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? How many jumps to reach 60?
Rabbit jumps 6 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? What is the smallest 3-digit number it lands on? How many jumps?
Kangaroo jumps 8 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? Are there numbers both the rabbit and kangaroo will touch?

homework.description: To reach 48, how many times did the rabbit jump? How many times did the kangaroo jump? What did you observe?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the hop-sequence model using a large number-line drawn on the board. Students call out landing numbers as the teacher draws the frog's jumps. Animal Jumps Q1, p.128 ("Frog jumps 3 steps at a time. Which numbers will the frog touch? Will it touch 67?") is posed and students record answers in their books, then share reasoning about 67.

Students work individually on Animal Jumps Q2, p.128 ("Squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? How many jumps to reach 60?"), filling the number-line ovals and answering the jump-count question. A brief whole-class check compares the squirrel's landing numbers with the frog's.

Pairs tackle Animal Jumps Q3, p.129 ("Rabbit jumps 6 steps at a time…smallest 3-digit number it lands on?") and Animal Jumps Q4, p.129 ("Kangaroo jumps 8 steps at a time…numbers both rabbit and kangaroo touch?") side by side, writing both hop sequences and circling shared numbers.

Class discussion: students share which numbers appeared in both sequences from Q4 and explain why. The teacher introduces the word 'multiple' for the numbers an animal lands on. Students note their observations in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Encourage students to articulate why 67 cannot be reached in steps of 3 — they should count on from the nearest multiple rather than just say 'no'. A common error is adding the step size to the wrong previous landing; pausing to say the sequence aloud before writing helps catch this. Animal Jumps Q5 and Q6 can serve as additional reasoning practice; Q5 is set as homework.
materials: Chalk number line drawn on the board (0–130 in steps of 2)

section_titles: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
periods.activity_title: Shared Landings: Finding Common Multiples from Animal Hops

tasks_in_class.description: To reach 60, how many times did the frog jump? How many times did the rabbit jump? What do you observe?
Which numbers do both the frog and the squirrel touch? A few common multiples of 3 and 4 are ___.
Which numbers do both the rabbit and the kangaroo touch? A few common multiples of 6 and 8 are ___.
Cat on 6, rat on 12. Cat jumps 3 steps, rat jumps 2 steps. Will the cat catch the rat? If yes, at which number?

homework.description: Find multiplication and division sentences in the number grid. Shade the sentences. How many can you find?

time_bands.activity: Using the hop sequences students built for the frog (multiples of 3) and the rabbit (multiples of 6), the class works through Animal Jumps Q6, p.130 ("To reach 60, how many times did the frog jump? How many times did the rabbit jump? What do you observe?"). Students write the division sentences 60÷3 and 60÷6 alongside their hop count.

Students list the frog's landing numbers and the squirrel's landing numbers side by side and circle numbers appearing in both lists for Common Multiples Q1, p.130 ("Which numbers do both the frog and the squirrel touch? A few common multiples of 3 and 4 are ___."). Repeat for Common Multiples Q2, p.130 ("Which numbers do both the rabbit and the kangaroo touch? A few common multiples of 6 and 8 are ___."), pairs then share their lists.

Pose the cat-and-rat chase in Common Multiples Q7, p.130 ("Cat on 6, rat on 12. Cat jumps 3 steps, rat jumps 2 steps. Will the cat catch the rat? If yes, at which number?"). Students track each animal's position step by step in a two-column table, then present conclusions. The teacher draws out the link to common multiples.

Brief consolidation: students write three common multiples of their choice of two numbers (e.g. 2 and 5) in their notebooks and explain in one sentence why those numbers appear in both hop sequences. The number-grid task is directed to homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The cat-and-rat puzzle is the informal entry point for the least common multiple idea; do not name LCM yet — let students describe it as 'the first number both animals land on.' A frequent error is listing multiples only up to 12 and concluding two numbers have no common multiple; prompt students to extend their lists. The number-grid shading task (Q8) works well as independent home activity.
materials: Two-column tracking table drawn on the board

section_titles: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
periods.activity_title: Gulabo's Garden: Arrays, Equal Groups, and Break-Apart

tasks_in_class.description: 12 lily flowers, each with 3 petals. How many petals? Use the 10+2 break-apart strategy.
Hibiscus has 5 petals. Gulabo counted 80 petals. How many flowers? Use the 5→10→50 build-up strategy.
Gulabo plants marigold saplings in a box. Count rows and columns from the picture. Write the mathematical statement.
Dailyfresh supermarket keeps strawberry boxes in a tray. Count columns and boxes per column from picture. Write the mathematical statement.
Complete arranging 18 cupcakes in two differently shaped trays given below.

homework.description: Find different ways of arranging 36, 8, 12, and 24 cupcakes in rows and columns in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Set the garden context and work through Gulabo's Garden Q1, p.131 ("12 lily flowers, each with 3 petals. How many petals? Use the 10+2 break-apart strategy.") as a class. Write 12×3 = (10+2)×3 = 30+6 = 36 on the board, then take Gulabo's Garden Q2, p.131 ("Hibiscus has 5 petals…80 petals…how many flowers?") — students use the build-up strategy in pairs.

Students examine the pictures for Gulabo's Garden Q3, p.132 ("Count rows and columns…write the mathematical statement") and Q4, p.132 ("Dailyfresh supermarket…count columns and boxes per column"), writing a multiplication sentence for each array. Pairs compare sentences and notice that rows×columns = columns×rows.

Students complete Gulabo's Garden Q5a, p.132 ("Complete arranging 18 cupcakes in two differently shaped trays") by drawing the cupcakes into the two tray outlines and writing multiplication statements for each arrangement. The class shares the two arrangements and discusses how the same total can be shown in different row/column shapes.

Quick recap: teacher draws a blank 3×5 grid on the board and asks students to write three things they know about it (total, multiplication sentence, a different arrangement with the same total). The open arrangement task for 36, 8, 12, and 24 is set as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: When writing multiplication statements from arrays, students often confuse which factor is the number of rows and which is the number of columns; affirm both orders as correct and use this to preview commutativity. The break-apart strategy in Q1 is the conceptual anchor for the formal algorithm the chapter builds toward — ensure every student writes out the partial products explicitly. Additional cupcake problems Q5b–Q5d can be used if the class moves quickly.
materials: Squared dot-grid paper for students to draw arrays

section_titles: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
periods.activity_title: Trays, Totals, and Doubling: Extending Multiplication Strategies

tasks_in_class.description: She can use two such trays in her oven at a time. How many cupcakes can she make in one attempt?
She has received a special order and made 108 cupcakes. How many trays has she baked?
Square baking tray holds 36 mini cupcakes. Complete the arrangement. Write number of columns, cupcakes per column, and multiplication statement.
Anvi doubled 23 flowers. How many are there now? Complete the before-and-after magic table for 10, 51, 95, 150, 199, 425, 500 and reverse for 222, 410, 500.
Guess the ones digit of the following numbers when doubled: 28, 56, 45, 17.
Give examples of numbers that when doubled give 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 in the ones place. Can we get 3, 5, 7, 9? Even or odd?

time_bands.activity: Building on the 18-cupcake tray work, students solve Gulabo's Garden Q5b, p.133 ("two trays at a time — how many cupcakes in one attempt?") and Q5c, p.133 ("108 cupcakes — how many trays?"), writing multiplication and division sentences. Then tackle Q5d, p.133 ("square tray of 36 mini cupcakes — complete the arrangement and write the statement"), drawing the array in squared notebooks.

Introduce Magician Anvi's doubling trick. Students complete The Doubling Magic (opening), p.134 ("Anvi doubled 23 flowers…complete the before-and-after table for 10, 51, 95, 150, 199, 425, 500; reverse for 222, 410, 500") individually, then check answers in pairs. Establish that doubling means multiplying by 2.

Class attempts The Doubling Magic Q1, p.134 ("Guess the ones digit when doubling 28, 56, 45, 17") — students predict first, then compute to verify. Move to Q2, p.134 ("Which doubled ones digits are possible? Can we get 3, 5, 7, 9?"). Students gather examples and make a conjecture about even results.

Students write their conjecture in one sentence: 'Doubling any whole number always gives an even number because…'. Two or three students read their reasoning aloud. Teacher affirms and names the pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write doubling as repeated addition (23+23) rather than ×2; both are correct but press them to also write the multiplication sentence. The key reasoning insight in Q2 is that the ones digit of any doubled number depends only on the ones digit of the original — this prepares the ones-digit cycle work in the multiplication table. The doubling drills (The Doubling Magic drills, p.134) for 32, 14, 26, 17, 39, 45 can be set as additional practice.
materials: Ganit mala or counters for doubling concretely

periods.activity_title: Inside the Multiplication Chart: Patterns and Properties

tasks_in_class.description: Fill each square in the 10×10 chart by multiplying the row number by the column number.
What do you notice about the numbers shaded in green? Why is this happening?
Are the numbers in row 7 the same as in column 7? In general, are numbers in a given row the same as in the corresponding column? Why?
Is there a row where all products are even numbers? Which rows have this property?
Is there a row having only odd numbers as products?
Are there rows that have both even and odd numbers? What do you notice? Why is it so?
Colour the common multiples of (a) 2 and 3, (b) 4 and 8, (c) 7 and 9 using different colours. Share observations.

time_bands.activity: Students fill the 10×10 multiplication chart, Multiplication Table (chart fill), p.135 ("Fill each square…multiplying row number by column number"), working at pace. Teacher circulates and points to the diagonal (1×1, 2×2…) as a self-check line.

Examine the green-shaded diagonal entries: Multiplication Table (green shading), p.135 ("What do you notice about the numbers shaded in green? Why is this happening?"). Then Q2, p.135 ("Are row 7 and column 7 the same?") — students compare and articulate the commutativity pattern in their own words.

Students investigate Q3, p.135 ("which rows are all-even?"), Q4, p.135 ("which rows are all-odd?"), and Q5, p.135 ("which rows have both?"), recording findings in a small table. Class discussion draws out: multiplying by an even number always gives even; multiplying by an odd number gives odd only when the other factor is also odd.

Students use coloured pencils to shade common multiples for Multiplication Table Q7, p.136 (pairs 2&3, 4&8, 7&9) and share one observation about each pair. This links the chart visually to the common-multiples idea from the animal jumps work.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse 'row' with 'column' when comparing row 7 to column 7; point physically to each before asking whether they match. The all-even-row result follows from the even × any = even rule — help students state this as a rule, not just an observation. Reasoning questions Q6, Q8–Q14 provide rich extension; select from them if the class advances quickly.

periods.activity_title: Ones-Digit Cycles and the Power of Multiplying by Tens

tasks_in_class.description: Observe the pattern in the ones digits of products in row 5. Observe other rows. What patterns do you notice?
Row 8 ones digits: 8,6,4,2,0,8,6,4,2,0. Guess the ones digit of 11×8, 12×8, 13×8. Verify by multiplying.
Count wheels in 10 tricycles (10×3), 10 more tricycles, and 20 tricycles. Fill blanks and notice the pattern.
Count wheels in 10 cars (10×4) and 30 cars (30×4). Fill blanks and notice the pattern.

time_bands.activity: Return to the filled multiplication chart. Students read out the ones digits of row 5 and row 8 for Multiplication Table Q8, p.136 ("Observe the pattern in the ones digits…what patterns do you notice?"). Then Q9, p.136 ("Row 8 ones digits cycle 8,6,4,2,0 — guess the ones digit of 11×8, 12×8, 13×8, then verify") — students predict, compute, and check.

Shift to the tricycle context: Multiples of Tens Q1, p.137 ("Count wheels in 10 tricycles, 10 more, and 20 tricycles — fill blanks and notice the pattern"). Students draw 10 tricycles as a group of boxes and count wheels, then repeat for 20. Discuss: how does the 10×3 fact help with 20×3?

Students work through Multiples of Tens Q2, p.137 ("Count wheels in 10 cars and 30 cars"), writing the multiplication statements and articulating the 'ten-times' pattern. Class shares: 30×4 = 3 tens × 4 = 12 tens = 120.

Students solve the paired fact set Multiples of Tens (solve set), p.137 ("10×6, 40×6, 10×8, 60×8, …") individually and compare with a partner. Teacher closes by asking: 'What changes and what stays the same when we move from 10×6 to 40×6?'

periods.teacher_notes: The ones-digit cycle in row 8 is the richest pattern in the table; make sure students predict before verifying — guessing ahead is the heart of the inquiry. When introducing multiples of tens, students frequently write 20×3=23 by annexing the digit rather than multiplying; using the decomposition 20×3 = (10+10)×3 = 30+30 makes the place-value logic visible. Reasoning questions Q10–Q14 on the ones-digit theme can extend the stronger students within this sitting.
materials: Completed multiplication charts from previous unit

periods.activity_title: Break It Apart: Multiplying 2-Digit Numbers Step by Step

tasks_in_class.description: Radha packs cupcakes in boxes of 4. She has packed 18 boxes. How many cupcakes? Use 10+8 decomposition.
8 bamboo rods needed for each bullock cart. How many rods for 23 carts? Use 20+3 decomposition.
25 geese and 12 sheep around a pond. Chippi the lizard sees many legs. How many legs does it see?
8 children sitting in each row, 15 such rows in an auditorium. How many children are in the auditorium?
A book shop has 9 books in each pile and 14 such piles. How many books does the shop have?

homework.description: Make your own stories for 34×3, 75×5, 46×6, 50×9 and find the products.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the structured partial-products table using Multiplying Using 10s Q1, p.138 ("Radha packs cupcakes in boxes of 4…18 boxes…how many cupcakes? Use 10+8 decomposition"). Teacher models filling the table row by row: 10×4=40, 8×4=32, total 72. Students then independently solve Q2, p.139 ("8 bamboo rods per bullock cart…23 carts…use 20+3 decomposition") using the same table.

Students work in pairs on Let Us Solve Q1, p.139 ("25 geese and 12 sheep…how many legs?") — they first identify the two separate multiplications needed, then apply the decomposition strategy for each. Pairs share working and class checks: 25×2 + 12×4.

Students solve Let Us Solve Q2, p.139 ("8 children per row, 15 rows") and Q3, p.139 ("9 books per pile, 14 piles") individually, writing full partial-product working. Teacher circulates and checks that the tens and ones partial products are written separately before adding.

Students call out one product from Q2 or Q3 and explain which two partial products they added. Story-making task (Q5) is set as homework — students choose any one of the four facts to begin a draft in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error at this stage is adding the partial products incorrectly by misaligning place values; writing 10×4 and 8×4 on separate rows of the table before summing prevents this. Let Us Solve Q4 (patchwork beads) and Q5 (story-making) are well-suited as extension within the unit or as homework. Encourage students to estimate the answer before computing — 15×8 is 'close to 15×10=150' — to develop a sense of magnitude.
materials: Partial-products table template drawn on the board

periods.activity_title: Taking Away in Chunks: The Partial Quotient Method

tasks_in_class.description: Factory ordered 58 wheels for tempos, each with 3 wheels. How many tempos can be made? Discuss thinking at each step.
Dairy farm: Chippi sees 88 legs. How many cows? Show work using the table, taking out groups of 10s.
In a big aquarium, Jolly fish sees 72 legs of octopuses. How many octopuses are there?
Sports store packs 4 shuttlecocks in a box. They have 50 shuttlecocks. How many full boxes? How many are left?
Rakul Chachi planted 75 rose saplings with 5 saplings per row. How many rows has she planted?

homework.description: Make stories for the following and solve: 70÷5, 84÷7, 69÷3, 93÷6.

time_bands.activity: Introduce division through the factory-wheels problem: Division Q1, p.140 ("58 wheels for tempos with 3 wheels each — how many tempos?"). Teacher models the partial-quotient table: subtract 10 groups of 3 (=30), remainder 28; subtract 9 groups of 3 (=27), remainder 1. Students record each step and count total groups: 19 tempos, 1 wheel left over.

Students attempt Division Q2, p.141 ("Chippi sees 88 legs — how many cows?") using the same step-by-step table, taking away groups of 10 fours at a time. Pairs compare tables and verify: 10 groups of 4 = 40, remaining 48; 10 groups of 4 = 40, remaining 8; 2 groups of 4 = 8. Total: 22 cows.

Students solve Let Us Solve Q1, p.141 ("72 legs of octopuses — how many octopuses?"), Q2, p.141 ("50 shuttlecocks in boxes of 4 — full boxes and remainder"), and Q3, p.141 ("75 rose saplings, 5 per row — how many rows?") individually. Teacher circulates to check that remainder is handled correctly in Q2.

Class shares the shuttlecock answer: 12 full boxes, 2 left over. Teacher distinguishes: sometimes a remainder is leftover (Q2), sometimes it means an extra partial group is needed — ask students to decide which applies in each context. Story-making task (Q4) set as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes stop at the first subtraction step and report the first partial group count as the full answer; emphasise continuing until the remainder is smaller than the divisor. Distinguish the 'share' reading (88 legs shared into groups of 4) from the 'measure' reading (how many groups of 4 fit into 88) — both appear in this section's problems. Story-making for division (Q4) is a strong homework task for consolidation.
materials: Partial-quotient table drawn on the board
Counters (optional, for students who need to act out grouping)

periods.activity_title: Hundreds, Decompose, Compute: Scaling Multiplication to 3 Digits

tasks_in_class.description: 100 bikes with 2 people each, 200 bikes; 100 cars with 4 people each, 500 cars. Fill in the blanks and describe how you found it.
125 autorickshaws carry 8 passengers each. How many passengers total? Use 100+20+5 decomposition.
Kahlu and Rabia pack 6 kulhads per box and packed 174 boxes. How many kulhads total? Use 100+70+4 decomposition.
BP Girl's school has 465 students and gives each two pencils on the first day. How many pencils does the school need to buy?

homework.description: 234 children organise a school mela, each contributing ₹5. How much money do they collect?

time_bands.activity: Students explore Multiples of 100 (bikes and cars), p.142 ("100 bikes with 2 people each, 200 bikes; 100 cars with 4 people each, 500 cars — fill blanks and describe"). They connect to the tens pattern: if 10×2=20 then 100×2=200. Then complete the pattern table, Multiples of 100 (pattern table), p.143, reading each triplet (1×3, 10×3, 100×3) and articulating the 'hundred-times' rule.

Introduce the 3-digit break-apart strategy with More Multiplication Q1, p.143–144 ("125 autorickshaws, 8 passengers each — use 100+20+5 decomposition"). Teacher writes three partial products: 100×8=800, 20×8=160, 5×8=40, then adds. Students copy the structure and verify the total.

Students apply the strategy independently to More Multiplication Q2, p.144 ("174 boxes, 6 kulhads per box — use 100+70+4 decomposition") and Let Us Solve Q1, p.144 ("465 students, 2 pencils each"). Pairs check each other's partial products before summing.

Quick class check of the 465×2 answer by estimation: '400×2=800, 60×2=120, 5×2=10 — should give 930.' Students state the rule in one sentence: 'Multiply hundreds, tens, and ones separately, then add.' The school mela problem is set as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The transition from 2-digit to 3-digit decomposition is conceptually identical; the only new move is the hundreds partial product. Students who learned the 2-digit break-apart strategy in the cupcake and bamboo-rod contexts transfer readily — name those contexts explicitly to activate prior knowledge. A common error is computing 100×8 as 800 but writing only 80; insisting on place-value labelling (8 hundreds = 800) prevents this.
materials: Board with three-row partial-products table template

periods.activity_title: Bigger Dividends, Smarter Splits: Extending Division and Discovering Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: 9 boats ferry 108 people equally. How many people per boat? Use partial quotient method (5+5+2).
7 buses take 245 children to the transport museum, each bus carrying the same number. How many children in each bus?
VentureOut took 259 people rafting on the Ganga. Each raft takes 7 people. How many rafts did it take?
Raju makes 8 auto trips a day. Which questions can be exactly calculated: (a) money per day? (b) trips in 7 days? (c) time per trip? (d) trips in 4 weeks?
₹30 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? ₹900 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? Draw arrows linking money and children.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Patterns in Division (sets A, B, C), p.146

tasks_in_class.description: Solve: (1) 60 tyres ÷ 6 = how many trucks? (2) 80 wheels ÷ 4 = how many cars? (3) 600 ant legs ÷ 6 = how many ants? (4) 800 rubber bands ÷ 4 rubber bands per packet = how many packets?

time_bands.activity: Work through the Cauvery ferry problem: More Division (Cauvery ferry), p.145 ("9 boats ferry 108 people — how many per boat? Use partial quotient 5+5+2 nines"). Teacher models the three-step table: 5×9=45, 5×9=45, 2×9=18, total 12. Students write and verify.

Students solve Let Us Solve Q1, p.147 ("245 children in 7 buses") and Q3, p.147 ("259 rafters in groups of 7") individually, then compare partial-quotient tables with a partner. Class checks both answers (35 children per bus; 37 rafts).

Pose the Raju problem: Let Us Solve Q5, p.147 ("8 auto trips a day — which of (a)–(d) can be exactly calculated?"). Small groups discuss which questions have enough information and which do not. Two groups share conclusions and reasoning.

Introduce Patterns in Division Q1–2, p.146 ("₹30 ÷ 3 and ₹900 ÷ 3 — draw arrows"). Students complete sets A, B, C (Patterns in Division sets A, B, C, p.146) and articulate: 'If 9÷3=3, then 90÷3=30 and 900÷3=300 — we move one or two places to the right.'

Students solve the four word problems in Patterns in Division (word problems), p.146 — trucks, cars, ants, rubber-band packets — applying the pattern directly. A quick round-the-class check closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students tackling 3-digit dividends with the partial quotient method sometimes take away groups that are too small and need many steps; prompt them to ask 'how many tens of nines fit?' before subtracting to keep the working compact. The Raju problem is excellent for critical thinking — the answer to 'money per day' requires information not given, so students must identify missing data rather than compute. The always/never/sometimes true table (Q7, p.148) and Anu's savings problem (Q4, p.147) can be used as extension if time allows.

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: Draw dots to show 4 rows with 5 dots in each row. Write the multiplication statement for your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Drawing shows 4 rows of 5 dots (20 dots total). Multiplication statement: 4 × 5 = 20.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the rows and count the dots in each row, then multiply rows by dots per row.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let students use counters to build the array first; stretch: ask them to write a second multiplication statement swapping rows and columns.

exercise.description: Gulabo plants marigold saplings in a box. Count rows and columns from the picture. Write the mathematical statement.

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: Priya wants to arrange 18 stickers in a tray with 3 rows. How many stickers will be in each row? Draw the arrangement and write the multiplication statement.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 stickers in each row. Drawing shows 3 rows of 6. Multiplication statement: 3 × 6 = 18.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total by the number of rows to find stickers per row, then draw the equal rows.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student 18 counters to physically arrange; stretch: ask for a second arrangement of 18 in a different number of rows.

exercise.description: Complete arranging 18 cupcakes in two differently shaped trays given below.

items.prompt: A bus has 4 wheels. How many wheels do 20 buses have?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 20 into two groups of 10, multiply each by 4, and add the results.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student added 4 to 20 instead of multiplying, confusing addition with multiplication.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student multiplied 20 by 20 (or 4 by 100), misapplying the tens pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student computed 10 × 4 = 40 and stopped at one group of ten buses instead of two.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 2 groups of 10 bus outlines and count wheels in each group; stretch: extend to 30 buses and explain the pattern.

exercise.description: Count wheels in 10 tricycles (10×3), 10 more tricycles, and 20 tricycles. Fill blanks and notice the pattern.

items.prompt: Each van carries 6 people. How many people do 100 vans carry?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the pattern: if 1 × 6 = 6 and 10 × 6 = 60, then 100 × 6 = 600.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student added 100 and 6 instead of multiplying.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student computed 10 × 6 rather than 100 × 6, confusing one zero with two.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student multiplied 100 by 10 rather than by 6, confusing the factors.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the triplet 1×6=6, 10×6=60, 100×6=? and let the student complete it; stretch: ask how many people 200 vans would carry.

exercise.description: 100 bikes with 2 people each, 200 bikes; 100 cars with 4 people each, 500 cars. Fill in the blanks and describe how you found it.

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A grasshopper jumps 5 steps at a time starting from 0. Will it ever land on 43? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. The grasshopper lands on 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, … These are all multiples of 5, which end in 0 or 5. Since 43 ends in 3 it is not a multiple of 5 and the grasshopper will never land on it.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 5 and check whether 43 appears by examining its ones digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the hop sequence on a number line up to 50; stretch: ask which number after 40 the grasshopper lands on, and how many jumps it takes.

exercise.description: Frog jumps 3 steps at a time. Which numbers will the frog touch? Will it touch 67?

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A deer jumps 8 steps at a time and a frog jumps 6 steps at a time, both starting from 0. Write two numbers that both animals will land on.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 72, … Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60, 66, 72, … Numbers both land on include 24 and 48 (and 72, etc.).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 8 and multiples of 6 and find numbers appearing in both lists.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a printed number line to 50 and let the student mark each animal's hops in different colours; stretch: find the smallest number both animals land on and explain why it is the smallest.

exercise.description: Kangaroo jumps 8 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? Are there numbers both the rabbit and kangaroo will touch?

items.prompt: A cat is at position 9 and jumps 3 steps each turn. A mouse is at position 15 and jumps 2 steps each turn. Will the cat ever land on the same number as the mouse? If yes, at which number?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cat's positions: 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, … Mouse's positions: 15, 17, 19, 21, … Both reach 21. Yes, the cat catches the mouse at 21.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track each animal's positions step by step and find the first number where both lists match.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give a two-column table and let the student fill in positions turn by turn; stretch: ask how many jumps each animal made to reach that number.

exercise.description: Cat on 6, rat on 12. Cat jumps 3 steps, rat jumps 2 steps. Will the cat catch the rat? If yes, at which number?

items.prompt: Manu doubles a number and the result has 6 in the ones place. Which of the following could be the original number?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13. Double of 13 = 26, which has 6 in the ones place.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Double the ones digit of each option and check which gives 6 in the ones place.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student doubled 14 to get 28 (ones digit 8, not 6), confusing which ones digit doubles to 6.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student doubled 23 to get 46 (ones digit 6 is correct) — wait, let me re-examine. 2×3=6. So 23 also doubles to 46. Reconsidering: 13 doubles to 26 (ones 6) and 23 doubles to 46 (ones 6) — both give ones digit 6.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write out 2×1 through 2×9 and circle which products end in 6; stretch: find two different numbers whose double ends in 6 and explain why.

exercise.description: Give examples of numbers that when doubled give 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 in the ones place. Can we get 3, 5, 7, 9? Even or odd?

items.prompt: Look at a multiplication table. Is 6 × 9 the same as 9 × 6? Write both products and explain why they are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 × 9 = 54 and 9 × 6 = 54. They are equal because the order of multiplication does not change the product — this is the same as swapping rows and columns in an array.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute both products and observe that row 6 column 9 and row 9 column 6 give the same entry in the multiplication table.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a 6×9 dot array, then rotate it to see 9×6; stretch: ask whether this is always true and give one more example to support the claim.

exercise.description: Are the numbers in row 7 the same as in column 7? In general, are numbers in a given row the same as in the corresponding column? Why?

items.prompt: The ones digits in the 8-times table follow the pattern 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0. What will be the ones digit of 15 × 8? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The ones digit of 15×8 is 0. The pattern 8,6,4,2,0 repeats every 5 steps. Position 15 is the 15th term; 15 ÷ 5 = 3 with no remainder, so it lands on the 5th position of the cycle, which is 0. Verify: 15×8 = 120, ones digit 0.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Extend the repeating ones-digit cycle 8,6,4,2,0 to the 15th term.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write out the ones digits for terms 1–15 in a strip and circle every 5th; stretch: predict the ones digit of 18×8 and explain.

exercise.description: Row 8 ones digits: 8,6,4,2,0,8,6,4,2,0. Guess the ones digit of 11×8, 12×8, 13×8. Verify by multiplying.

items.prompt: Meena says: 'I can find out how many weeks are in 56 days.' Ravi says: 'I cannot find out how many hours Meena sleeps in 56 days.' Who is right, and why?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both are right. 56 ÷ 7 = 8 weeks — all the information needed (56 days, 7 days per week) is given. The number of hours Meena sleeps per day is not given, so Ravi's calculation cannot be done exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether all numbers needed for the calculation are given in the problem.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to list what numbers they need for each calculation, then check which are given; stretch: ask the student to write a question about 56 days that can be exactly calculated and one that cannot.

exercise.description: Raju makes 8 auto trips a day. Which questions can be exactly calculated: (a) money per day? (b) trips in 7 days? (c) time per trip? (d) trips in 4 weeks?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 100. The pattern: 7÷7=1, 70÷7=10, 700÷7=100. Each time the dividend is ten times larger, the quotient is ten times larger.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the place-value pattern: dividing a multiple of 100 by the same single-digit divisor gives a quotient 100 times the basic fact.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student repeated the quotient of 70÷7=10, not scaling up for the extra zero.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student multiplied the quotient by 100 instead of recognising it is already scaled by 100.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student gave the quotient of the previous step (70) rather than computing 700÷7.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the three-step pattern 7÷7, 70÷7, 700÷7 in a column and ask the student to describe what changes each time; stretch: ask what 7000÷7 would be and explain.

exercise.description: ₹30 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? ₹900 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? Draw arrows linking money and children.

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A rabbit jumps 4 steps at a time starting from 0. How many jumps does it take to reach 36?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count multiples of 4 until reaching 36, or divide 36 by 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write out the sequence 4, 8, 12, … and count; stretch: ask how many jumps to reach 60 and how many more jumps from 36 to 60.

exercise.description: Squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? How many jumps to reach 60?

items.prompt: Using the multiplication table, find the product of 7 and 8.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate row 7 and column 8 in the multiplication chart; the entry is 56.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count in 7s up to the 8th multiple; stretch: verify that 8×7 gives the same answer and name the property.

exercise.description: Fill each square in the 10×10 chart by multiplying the row number by the column number.

items.prompt: Shade all the common multiples of 3 and 6 that appear in the multiplication table up to 10×10. Write three numbers you shaded.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Common multiples of 3 and 6 up to 100: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60, 66, 72, 78, 84, 90, 96. Any three of these are correct. (All multiples of 6 are also multiples of 3.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 6 — every multiple of 6 is automatically a multiple of 3, so shade all multiples of 6 in the chart.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a blank 10×10 chart and let the student shade multiples of 3 in one colour and multiples of 6 in another; stretch: explain why every multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 3.

exercise.description: Colour the common multiples of (a) 2 and 3, (b) 4 and 8, (c) 7 and 9 using different colours. Share observations.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly completes the pattern? 3 × 5 = 15, 30 × 5 = 150, 300 × 5 = ___

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1500. 300 × 5 = 1500 (one hundred times 15).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Extend the pattern: each step multiplies the first factor by 10, so the product is also multiplied by 10.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student added 5 to 150 rather than multiplying, confusing the operation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student repeated the previous step's product (150) without scaling up for the extra zero.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student scaled by 100 twice instead of once, giving 10 times the correct answer.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the triplet vertically and circle how many zeros are in each first factor; stretch: predict the next step (3000 × 5) and explain.

items.prompt: Using the division pattern, find: 600 ÷ 4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 150. Since 6 ÷ 4 does not divide evenly, use 60 ÷ 4 = 15 and then 600 ÷ 4 = 150.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find 6 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 2, so use the pattern from 60 ÷ 4 = 15, then 600 ÷ 4 = 150.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the two-step pattern 60÷4=15 first and then ask what 600÷4 must be; stretch: verify by multiplying 150×4 and explaining why the answer should equal 600.

exercise.book_ref: Patterns in Division (sets A, B, C), p.146

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: A flower has 4 petals. There are 14 flowers in a vase. How many petals are there in total?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Break 14 into 10 + 4, multiply each part by 4, and add the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw 14 flowers with 4 petals each and count; stretch: ask how many petals if 3 more flowers are added.

exercise.description: 12 lily flowers, each with 3 petals. How many petals? Use the 10+2 break-apart strategy.

items.prompt: A shelf holds 6 books. There are 17 shelves in the library. How many books are in the library?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 17 into 10 + 7, multiply each part by 6, then add the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the partial-products table with two rows (10×6 and 7×6) and let the student fill in; stretch: ask how many books if there are 27 shelves instead.

exercise.description: Radha packs cupcakes in boxes of 4. She has packed 18 boxes. How many cupcakes? Use 10+8 decomposition.

items.prompt: There are 9 seats in each row of a hall. There are 16 rows. How many seats are in the hall?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 16 into 10 + 6, multiply each by 9, and add the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: offer a partial-products table template with the first row (10×9=90) already filled; stretch: ask how many rows would be needed if the hall requires 180 seats.

exercise.description: 8 children sitting in each row, 15 such rows in an auditorium. How many children are in the auditorium?

items.prompt: A baker has 65 bread rolls. She packs 3 rolls in each bag. How many full bags can she fill? How many rolls are left over?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 21 full bags with 2 rolls left over. 65 ÷ 3: take 10 groups of 3 = 30, remainder 35; take 10 more groups of 3 = 30, remainder 5; take 1 more group of 3 = 3, remainder 2. Total groups: 21, remainder 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the partial quotient method, taking away groups of 10 threes at a time until the remainder is less than 3.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the partial-quotient table template and guide the student through one step; stretch: ask how many more rolls are needed to fill one more bag.

exercise.description: Factory ordered 58 wheels for tempos, each with 3 wheels. How many tempos can be made? Discuss thinking at each step.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper has 68 mangoes. He puts 4 mangoes in each basket. How many full baskets can he make? How many mangoes are left over?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 17 full baskets, 0 mangoes left over. 68 ÷ 4: take 10 groups of 4 = 40, remainder 28; take 7 groups of 4 = 28, remainder 0. Total: 17 baskets.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the partial quotient method, subtracting groups of 10 fours then smaller groups until no remainder.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use counters to physically group 68 objects into fours; stretch: ask how many baskets would be needed for 80 mangoes and explain the difference.

exercise.description: Sports store packs 4 shuttlecocks in a box. They have 50 shuttlecocks. How many full boxes? How many are left?

items.prompt: A factory makes 7 chairs every hour. It works for 136 hours in a month. How many chairs does it make?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 136 into hundreds, tens, and ones, multiply each part by 7, then add the three partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a three-row partial-products table and let the student fill in 100×7, 30×7, 6×7 before adding; stretch: ask how many chairs in 2 months if the same rate is kept.

exercise.description: 125 autorickshaws carry 8 passengers each. How many passengers total? Use 100+20+5 decomposition.

items.prompt: A school has 126 students and divides them equally into 9 groups for a sports day. How many students are in each group?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 14 students per group. 126 ÷ 9: take 5 groups of 9 = 45, remainder 81; take 5 more groups of 9 = 45, remainder 36; take 4 groups of 9 = 36, remainder 0. Total: 14 groups.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the partial quotient method, subtracting groups of five nines at a time until the remainder is zero.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the partial-quotient table and show the first step (5×9=45 removed); stretch: ask what happens if one more student joins — can they still be divided equally into 9 groups?

exercise.description: 9 boats ferry 108 people equally. How many people per boat? Use partial quotient method (5+5+2).

items.prompt: A farmer packs 5 oranges in each crate. He has 400 oranges. How many crates does he need?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 80 crates. Since 4 ÷ 5 is not whole, use 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so 400 ÷ 5 = 80.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the place-value division pattern: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so 400 ÷ 5 = 80.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the pattern 40÷5=8 first and ask what 400÷5 must be; stretch: ask how many crates for 800 oranges and explain the pattern.

exercise.description: Solve: (1) 60 tyres ÷ 6 = how many trucks? (2) 80 wheels ÷ 4 = how many cars? (3) 600 ant legs ÷ 6 = how many ants? (4) 800 rubber bands ÷ 4 rubber bands per packet = how many packets?
